heading: Test units
body:
ty test finds every server/tests/<Name>Test.<ext> and client/tests/<Name>Test.<ext> file in the project. Each of these files is a test unit. ty test compiles each one like any other entry. Then it runs the driver (the code that runs the test cases) that the compiler wrote for it. It prints one line per case, then a total. It exits with a non-zero code if a case fails. CI (continuous integration) can use that exit code. A Yon unit runs through the same supervisor that serves a route. That is why all Yon languages report through one path. A Tac unit runs in its own realm. JavaScript and TypeScript units run under Bun or Node. Dart units run on the Dart VM. Swift, Kotlin, C#, F# and Rust units run as a compiled binary. Go units run with go run, Ruby units run under CRuby, and Lua units run with the `lua` program.

Every public method of an annotated class needs a test case that calls it, and the development server checks this rule. A Setup and an HTTPClient are not in this list: Tachyon calls a Setup itself, and Tachyon writes the methods of a client. When no test* case called one of these methods, ty preview still starts, and it lists the missing ones in the terminal and in the error box of open pages (`TY2023`), for example `no test case called GreetingService.message`. A class-level marker says that the type has behavior the framework owns. So its public methods are the contract (the promised behavior) of the application. It costs the least to find an untested contract while you work. ty serve and ty start do not run tests or check this record. Use ty test --coverage as the CI gate before serving a release: it fails. TAC_ALLOW_UNTESTED=1 skips the check for one run. ty test prints the same report. With --coverage it fails on that report (`TY2022`), which is the form CI needs.

A method is covered only when a test case really called it while ty test ran. A test that only writes the name of the method does not cover it. In a test build, and only there, the compiler adds one line at the start of each public method of an annotated class, and of each public static method of a utility class. That line records the call. A Tac JavaScript or TypeScript utility that another file imports by its path, or that uses `import.meta`, loads as its own module, so the test build cannot add that line to it yet; ty test leaves such a utility out of the report instead of calling it untested. A production build has no such line, so the recording costs nothing in production. Each case reports the methods that it called, and ty test keeps the first case that called each one. A call inside the real class counts, also when the test calls another method or a real Needs dependency that calls it. A call on a Fake does not count, because a Fake is not the real class. So a controller test that fakes GreetingService does not cover GreetingService.message: a unit for the service must call it. ty test --coverage lists every class with its called methods, the first case that called each one, and the methods that no case called.

ty test writes the calls to `.tachyon/coverage/calls.json`. ty preview reuses this record only when its test run succeeded and no role file or test is newer. Before a new test run, ty marks the old record unsuccessful. If it cannot write that change, it stops before running any cases. This means that a failed or interrupted run cannot leave an older success in place. A record with no successful run, including an older record without this field, makes ty preview run the test units once before it starts. A failing test shows `TY2020` in the error box, even when it called every required method. Successful automatic tests are quiet: the first stdout line is still the server-ready message. Run ty test explicitly to see each case and its total. A write error on the record is `TY2024`. If the test units of a language cannot run on this machine, for example Swift units where swiftc is missing, ty cannot record their calls. Then, for that language only, it uses a name check: a case in a unit that names the class must also name the method. The report marks these classes with `[name check]`. This fallback describes coverage only: it does not make a failed run successful. Methods that the compiler writes are exempt (they need no test), because they contain no logic that a person wrote. A derived Store query, a declared HTTP request method and a Convert are all only a signature without a body. A signature is a name and types. ty init creates a service, a controller, a Setup in each tests folder and the units that call the service and the controller. So a new project starts with all checks passing.

A service that uses Tachyon's browser APIs, such as `Clock` or `Geolocation`, gets fake answers in a unit: a `@Fake` field in JavaScript and TypeScript, and `BrowserFakes` in Go, Ruby, Swift, C# and F# (see "Browser APIs in test units").

Controller methods count too, because a test can reach them. A unit in server/tests can use every controller in server/controllers, in the same way that it uses a service. In JavaScript, TypeScript and Ruby, construct(GreetingController) makes the controller and gives it the fakes for its Needs fields, and in Lua `self:construct(GreetingController)` does the same. In the other Yon languages, the unit makes the controller directly, for example GreetingController() in Python. The test then calls the controller method directly, without HTTP. Step 5 of Your first app shows a controller test.

Before it runs, the command checks the runtimes that its units need, as the development server does. A TypeScript unit may be under a runtime that supports only JavaScript. Then it reports the readiness diagnostic, not the runtime's own error message. If you are not sure that a toolchain works, run ty doctor first.
